_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and BC Indigenous nations are using technology on their own terms — for language revitalization, land stewardship, cultural preservation, and self-determined governance. We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Greens Leader Emily Lowan, CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, B.C. Conservatives Leader Lorne Doerkson, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby and OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie. Amid the avalanche of policy announcements, platform promises and attack ads, it can be hard to know where party leaders really stand on the issues. Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. In a poll conducted on Oct. 13, the economy/jobs was the top issue for 25 per cent of respondents; housing/poverty/homelessness for 23 per cent; healthcare for 21 per cent, and crime/public safety for nine per cent. With the cost of living the top issue for most voters, economic concerns moved to the forefront as the campaigns hit the home stretch. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. After 10 years in power, the NDP is defending its economic record amid historic deficits. The party’s main new plank is a proposed income tax hike on the wealthiest 3.88 per cent of British Columbians. The NDP says it would spend the extra money on new health-care facilities, child care centres and schools, slowly lowering the deficit over the next three years. The B.C. Conservative Party promises to cut taxes by raising the personal income tax exemption. This would essentially give everyone a $1,000 break. The party also promises new spending and a reduced deficit. Much of this relies on extremely optimistic economic growth, far beyond what banks and academic experts forecast. The B.C. items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
